description: Power Integrations, Inc. designs, develops, manufactures, and markets analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits, and other electronic components and circuitry used in high-voltage power conversion.
description_full: Power Integrations, Inc. designs, develops, manufactures, and markets analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits, and other electronic components and circuitry used in high-voltage power conversion. It provides a range of alternating current to direct current power conversion products that address power supply up to approximately 500 watts of output for consumer appliances, utility meters, LCD monitors, tablets, smartphones, computers, TVs, consumer and industrial applications, and LED lightings; and power conversion in high-power applications comprising industrial motors, solar and wind-power systems, electric locomotives, and high-voltage DC transmission systems. The company also offers InnoSwitch IC for electric vehicles; high-voltage gate-driver products used to operate high-voltage switches, such as insulated-gate bipolar transistors and silicon-carbide MOSFETs under the SCALE and SCALE-2 product-family names; and SCALE-iDriver for use in powertrain and charging applications for electric vehicles. In addition, it provides motor-driver ICs for use in refrigerator compressors, ceiling fans, air purifiers, and circulation pumps, as well as pumps and fans used in appliances, such as dishwashers, laundry machines, and boilers. The company serves communications, computer, consumer, and industrial markets. It sells its products to original equipment manufacturers and merchant power supply manufacturers through direct sales staff, as well as a network of independent sales representatives and distributors in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific. Power Integrations, Inc. was incorporated in 1988 and is headquartered in San Jose, California.

financial_summary: Power Integrations, Inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $2.2B market cap on $444M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -12% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 11% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 51% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $87M in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.05× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -11.6% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 6.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 2% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.10x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-41.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 49% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 34% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 56% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 61% and a beta of 1.24, it amplifies market moves.
About $36.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 27% in the 2020 crash, 36% in the 2022 bear market and 58% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $22.11 (margin of safety -82%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $17.41 to $29.03 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 51.0 vs 26.7 and EV/EBITDA 26.7 vs 16.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 514% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $74.00 on average, 84% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.9%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.77).
It runs a 51% gross margin and converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow, or 11% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-11.6% of assets).
ROE of 3% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 22.8% of revenue on R&D and 8.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $249.5M (11% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 16.0, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 255 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -12.0% over 3 years, -1.9% over 5 years and 2.6% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.6% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 5.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.7%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (16 sales, net $28.3M sold).
It returns 6.5% a year to shareholders (4.4% in buybacks and 2.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 193% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 13.1% of the float, 6.5 days to cover.
people: With about 877 employees, each generates about $506K of revenue, 1.4x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 2.6% a year.
That works out to $99K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $592K (1x revenue per employee).
